The model in `vignette("flexyBayes-01-mixed-models")` is the same model
ASReml fits. What changes here is how its parameters are described.

# One sentence

REML returns a point estimate for each variance component and a standard
error. A Bayesian fit returns a **distribution** for each one, and every
statement -- an interval, a heritability, a probability that one genotype
beats another -- is read off that distribution rather than derived from an
asymptotic argument about it.

# The prior

Before seeing data you state what values a parameter could plausibly take.
That is the prior. It is combined with the likelihood to give the posterior.

flexyBayes sets a weakly-informative default scaled to your response, and
tells you what it chose:


``` r
fit <- flexybayes(
  fixed   = yield ~ rep,
  random  = ~ rep:block + gen,
  data    = john.alpha,
  backend = "inla"
)
#> 
#> -- flexyBayes: INLA fit ----------------------------------------
#>   formula: yield ~ 1 + rep + f(rep_block_id, model = "iid", <prior: uniform-SD(0, 3.049)>) + f(gen, model = "iid", <prior: uniform-SD(0, 3.049)>)
#>   family:  gaussian
#> ------------------------------------------------------------

prior_summary(fit)
#> <prior_summary>  backend = inla
#>   Source: auto-default bounded uniform on SD (weakly-informative; half-Cauchy advised for small J)
#>     Upper bound U = 3.049069
#>     Scale basis    = identity_sd_uniform
#>     prior_fixed_sd:  not supplied -- the fixed effects carry INLA's own control.fixed defaults -- prec = 0.001 on the slopes (a standard deviation near 32), and prec.intercept = 0, which is flat
#> 
#> <fb_prior> 3 specifications
#>   sigma ~ uniform(lower = 0, upper = 3.049069)
#>   sd(group = "rep:block") ~ uniform(lower = 0, upper = 3.049069)
#>   sd(group = "gen") ~ uniform(lower = 0, upper = 3.049069)
```

Two things about that default are worth stating plainly.

It is a **choice**, and a different choice gives a different answer. With
plenty of data the difference is negligible, because the likelihood dominates.
With a variance estimated from a handful of levels it is not negligible at
all, and that is the case where it earns its place.

Where an engine's own default would be used instead, the `prior` column of
`summary()` says `engine default` rather than naming a prior the fit never
saw. A structure whose hyperparameters have no standard-deviation slot -- the
unstructured and factor-analytic covariances on INLA -- is reported that way.

# The posterior


``` r
summary(fit)$varcomp[, c("component", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
#> Bayesian mixed model summary  [flexyBayes / inla]
#> ============================================================== 
#>   Fixed    : yield ~ rep 
#>   Random   : ~rep:block + gen 
#>   Model    : G: block within rep; gen iid; R: units 
#>   Family   : gaussian / identity 
#>   Representation: exact (model, not inference)
#>   Engine:         INLA Laplace
#>   N        : 72 design rows, 72 observed responses
#>   na_action: augment; 0 missing response(s); 0 cell(s) completed
#>   Runtime  : 1.5 sec
#> 
#> -- Fixed effects (posterior mean, 95% credible interval) --------
#>         term estimate std.error conf.low conf.high
#>  (Intercept)   4.5182    0.1598   4.2016    4.8349
#>        repR2   0.2978    0.1936  -0.0887    0.6844
#>        repR3  -0.4140    0.1936  -0.8006   -0.0275
#> 
#> -- Variance components (95% credible interval) ------------------
#> Estimate = posterior mean (not REML). Prior column is the prior that was used.
#>     component estimate std.error conf.low conf.high
#>         sigma   0.2926    0.0364   0.2290    0.3716
#>  sd_rep:block   0.2880    0.0779   0.1632    0.4677
#>        sd_gen   0.3974    0.0734   0.2736    0.5610
#>                          prior note
#>  uniform(lower=0, upper=3.049)     
#>  uniform(lower=0, upper=3.049)     
#>  uniform(lower=0, upper=3.049)     
#> 
#> -- Hyperparameters (INLA, precision scale) ---------------------
#>                                            mean     sd 0.025quant 0.5quant
#> Precision for the Gaussian observations 12.2230 3.0395     7.2296  11.8925
#> Precision for rep_block_id              14.9651 8.7757     4.5831  12.8732
#> Precision for gen                        7.0003 2.6399     3.1726   6.5569
#>                                         0.975quant    mode
#> Precision for the Gaussian observations    19.1161 11.2912
#> Precision for rep_block_id                 37.7820  9.6123
#> Precision for gen                          13.4059  5.7509
#> 
#> -- Convergence -----------------------------------------------
#>   Engine    : INLA nested Laplace approximation
#>   Mode status: 0 (0 = converged)
#>   Marginal log-likelihood: -65.806
#>   Largest symmetric KLD between the Gaussian approximation and the
#>   corrected marginal: 3.81e-07
#>   Numerical confirm: PASS
#>      component  estimate  conf.low conf.high
#> 1        sigma 0.2926117 0.2289789 0.3715709
#> 2 sd_rep:block 0.2880204 0.1631987 0.4677452
#> 3       sd_gen 0.3973737 0.2736067 0.5610298
```

`estimate` is the posterior mean. The interval is a **credible interval**: on
this model and this prior, the parameter lies inside it with probability 0.95.
That is the statement most people believe a confidence interval makes, and
here it is the statement being made.

# Why it matters in practice

## Any function of the parameters is exact

Heritability is a ratio of variances. In REML you get it by substituting the
estimates and propagating the standard errors with the delta method, which
linearises the ratio and assumes normality on a scale where neither holds
near a boundary. That is how an ASReml heritability acquires a standard error
implying an interval below zero.

Here the ratio is computed on every draw, so its posterior is exact and
cannot leave the range the function maps into:


``` r
h2 <- vpredict(fit, h2 ~ sd_gen^2 / (sd_gen^2 + sigma^2), draws = TRUE)
range(h2[, "h2"])
#> [1] 0.2960232 0.8983319
quantile(h2[, "h2"], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>      2.5%       50%     97.5% 
#> 0.4197655 0.6432970 0.8053794
```

Every draw lies in `[0, 1]`, so the interval does. No asymptotics were used.

On the INLA path these draws come from the fitted joint hyperparameter
posterior rather than from the integration grid the fit was assembled on. The
distinction matters only in the tails, and only for a functional -- but that
is precisely where an interval is read.

## A variance near zero stays honest

REML can put a variance component exactly at zero and report a small standard
error beside it, which reads as certainty that the effect is absent. It is
usually a boundary, not a finding. flexyBayes reports a component that has run
to the boundary as unidentified, with a warning naming the term, rather than
as a confident zero.

## Small trials are where the difference bites

With many levels per variance component the posterior mean sits close to the
REML estimate and the interval close to the Wald interval. With few levels
they diverge, the asymptotic argument behind REML's standard error is weakest,
and the prior is doing real work. `vignette("flexyBayes-04-illustration")`
degrades a complete trial on purpose to show how far apart they get.

# What it costs

Approximation, or time, and you choose which. The INLA path approximates the
posterior and returns in seconds. The brms path samples it and returns in
minutes. For the models in this package the two agree on the certified
overlap class, and the package reports which engine answered.
